3:As AI coding agents carry out development tasks with greater autonomy, developers are shifting from direct implementation toward supervising delegated work. Yet existing research offers limited understanding of how developers organize supervisory activities into connected workflows. Drawing on observations and workflow diagrams from 19 experienced developers, we reconfigure Sheridan’s framework of human supervisory control into seven stages and the connecting loops for supervising AI coding agents. We applied the framework to public developer discussions on Reddit and found that supervisory demands extend across stages and that developers manage them by concentrating effort in planning, delegating supervisory work to other agents, and turning recurring guidance into reusable assets. Our framework provides a useful analytical lens for understanding how developers supervise AI coding agents by capturing how supervision is structured in agentic software development.
11:This motivates a central question for our work: How do developers organize supervision over the course of a task delegated to AI coding agents? To answer this, we developed a framework for supervising AI coding agents by reconfiguring Sheridan’s framework (Figure 1 ). The framework was based on a qualitative study with 19 experienced developers, where we observed participants working with agents and asked them to reconstruct their supervision workflows as diagrams. Our analysis identified seven supervisory stages— Plan , Monitor , Wait , Review , Teach , Manual Fix , and Update Assets —and loops connecting them. Together, these stages and loops capture how supervision is organized in agentic software development, providing an analytic lens for studying developer supervision of AI coding agents.
13:We then applied the framework to developer discussions on Reddit to examine supervisory patterns across the development process. We identified three demands that span multiple stages: maintaining alignment between agent behavior and developer intent, enforcing quality beyond task completion, and maintaining understanding of agents’ work. We also found three strategies for managing these demands: concentrating effort in planning, distributing supervisory work to other agents, and externalizing repeated supervision into reusable assets. Through the framework, we show how supervisory demands extend across stages and how developers redistribute their effort in response.
17:Over the past few months we've responded to this shift by improving the efficiency of Cursor's agent harness. The harness gives us direct control over how each request is assembled, how context is reused, and when work is divided across agents. Changes across each of these layers reduced token costs for users by 7% without reducing agent quality.
37:To decide which tools to keep in static context, we A/B tested several configurations based on how often each tool was used and whether models needed to see it from the start. We tracked token usage, cost, latency, tool-call errors, and overall agent usage to make sure the savings did not degrade quality.
83:These changes reduced the rate of cold cache misses by 20%.
99:This kind of context isolation between agents and subagents does carry a coordination tax, though, because agents that do not share context can duplicate work or pursue tasks that are no longer necessary.

Where repositories differ, it adapts. A diff is not a shipped change, so when CI fails, it reacts. 11:We introduce AgentSWE , a benchmark that turns faithful delegation from anecdote into measurement ( Figure 1 ) through three commitments. The first is to measure the whole lifecycle, through twenty-five tasks spanning all three stages. Ten Creation tasks commission a complete agent from a natural-language requirement, over workloads from GUI automation to formal theorem proving, each scoped against a mature open-source system; ten Editing tasks ask for new capabilities in the pinned codebase of a production agent such as OpenHands or Aider, capabilities that cut through crash recovery, permission fencing, and transactional state; and five Optimization tasks set a working agent against a measurable target. The second commitment is that evaluation should mirror the delegation it studies. Each task is framed as a commission: the builder sees only what a customer could provide, while acceptance also tests the stated clauses its examples leave out. The builder develops against the requirement and a few illustrative cases; held-out cases then test the frozen delivery in isolation. The third commitment follows from the absence of a prescribed reference implementation: every Creation and Editing execution is graded against a rubric derived from the requirement itself, and hard gates assign zero to invalid executions and inapplicable patches.
13:We put this instrument to work on five models as builders in the Codex harness, together with further pairings of harness and model. The verdict is sobering. The strongest builders average 19.1 on Creation and 31.6 on Editing, and in Optimization no builder closes more than 5 % of the remaining gap to the target on average, and only 13 of the 25 runs score above their starter. Creation runs that end development at 90 or above deliver agents averaging 9.9 on held-out cases. The gap between what a builder demonstrates and what it delivers is not the corner case of agent software engineering; it is the norm. The builders’ trajectories reveal recurring failures. Builders overfit to the visible development cases, and the delivery fails on the clauses those cases leave out; they ship hollow runtimes, code that reads as complete but does no work when run; and both builders and the agents they deliver claim completions that their own records contradict. Each of these modes names a habit that the next generation of coding agents can be built and trained to avoid. More development cases, a prescribed design, an instruction to test, and a longer case budget shift the scores but leave held-out Result low under every condition.
